extracted.intended_audience: JOSS reviewers / peer reviewers of research software submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for reviewers evaluating submissions to the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS), covering repository practices, documentation, software functionality, and required paper sections. Intended to guide reviewers in accepting, requesting minor revisions, or requesting major revisions for JOSS submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper core content
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOSS paper (the compiled PDF associated with this submission) should only include: a list of the authors of the software and their affiliations; a summary describing the high-level functionality and purpose of the software for a diverse, non-specialist audience; a clear statement of need that illustrates the purpose of the software; a description of how this software compares to other commonly-used packages in this research area; mentions (if applicable) of any ongoing research projects using the software or recent scholarly publications enabled by it; and a list of key references including a link to the software archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the paper should not include software documentation such as API functionality, as this should be outlined in the software documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software license (OSI-approved license present)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be an OSI approved license included in the repository. Common licenses such as those listed on choosealicense.com are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable: A plain-text LICENSE or COPYING file with the contents of an OSI approved license. Not acceptable: A phrase such as 'MIT license' in a README file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that the software demonstrates clear research impact or credible scholarly significance and shows evidence of meaningful contribution to the research community rather than being a one-off tool for a single analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals of research impact or scholarly significance may include: published research citing or using the software; evidence of adoption by other research groups; integration into established research workflows or pipelines; demonstrated performance improvements or novel capabilities compared to alternatives; clear potential for reuse and citation by other researchers. The decision on scope and significance is ultimately made by JOSS editors; reviewers should flag questionable scope to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development timeline (sustained development)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project should show evidence of sustained development over time (preferably months or years) rather than rapid, recent code generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for: commit history spanning an extended period, iterative improvements and refinements, and evolution of features and capabilities. Good: commits distributed over 6+ months showing gradual feature development. OK: development spanning 6+ months but with sporadic or bursty activity. Not acceptable: all or most commits concentrated in the last few weeks before submission. If clear failures are found early (e.g., repo made public days before submission), flag to the handling editor rather than proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open development (public history and engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should have been developed openly from early stages. For recently created public repositories, there should be at least six months of public development history with evidence of releases or version tags, public issues and/or pull requests, and ideally external engagement from users or contributors outside the core team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: repository public from inception with documented releases and community interaction. OK: repository made public 6+ months ago with clear evidence of ongoing development. Not acceptable: repository made public immediately before submission with limited public development history. Private prior development may be acceptable if authors demonstrate substantial prior effort and public availability for at least six months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative effort (contributors and code review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commit history should show contributions from multiple developers and evidence of iterative refinement through community feedback (multiple contributors, code review through pull requests, responses to issues and feature requests, evidence of community-driven improvements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: multiple developers contributing with evidence of iterative refinement via issues and PRs. OK: single author but shows other evidence of community engagement (in repo or paper). Not acceptable: single author with no evidence of community engagement, external use, or collaborative input. For single-author projects, the paper can supply evidence of community use; the author list and collaborators may also be signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good open-source practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The project should demonstrate it is a reusable, non-throwaway research software project that follows good open-source practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements: license (OSI-approved), documentation (README, installation instructions, usage examples, API documentation), quality assurance (automated tests, CI, or documented verification), releases (tagged versions or formal release process), community pathways (clear contribution guidelines and support channels). Good: all elements present and well-maintained. OK: core elements present (license, docs, tests, contribution guidelines). Bad (not acceptable): missing critical elements or appears to be a one-time code dump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository documentation: README and statement of need
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be sufficient documentation (README or equivalent) for the reviewer to understand core functionality. The README should include a statement of need explaining what problems the software solves, who the target audience is, and its relation to other work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be clear about problem, audience, and context. This criterion overlaps with the paper's 'Statement of need' but applies to repository-level documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation instructions and dependency management
rubrics_metrics.description: Software dependencies should be clearly documented and their installation handled by an automated procedure where possible. Installation should follow established distribution and dependency management approaches for the language used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: software is simple to install and follows established distribution/packaging conventions (e.g., pip-installable for Python). OK: a list of dependencies plus a script (e.g., Makefile) to handle installation. Bad (not acceptable): dependencies are unclear, and/or installation lacks automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example usage (realistic examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should include examples of how to use the software, ideally to solve real-world analysis problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples should help reviewers and users exercise core functionality; they should be realistic and illustrative of common use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: API documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should check that the software API is documented to a suitable level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: all functions/methods are documented including example inputs and outputs. OK: core API functionality is documented. Bad (not acceptable): API is undocumented. The decision is left to reviewer discretion based on experience with the software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community guidelines (contribution and support)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be clear guidelines for third-parties wishing to contribute to the software, report issues or problems, or seek support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for CONTRIBUTING.md, issue templates, or other documentation that lowers friction for community engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality verification (install & test core features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are expected to install the software they are reviewing and to verify the core functionality of the software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If installation or verification is impossible, document the issue in the review. Functionality checks may be manual or automated but must be objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and quality assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are strongly encouraged to include an automated test suite covering the core functionality of their software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: automated test suite hooked up to continuous integration (GitHub Actions, CircleCI, etc.). OK: documented manual steps that can be followed to objectively check expected functionality (e.g., sample input files). Bad (not acceptable): no way for the reviewer to objectively assess whether the software works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper: Statement of need (required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must have a clearly labeled 'Statement of need' section that states what problems the software is designed to solve, identifies the target audience, and explains the software's relation to other work in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: clear problem statement, well-defined target audience, and context within the broader field. OK: addresses key elements but could be more specific. Bad (not acceptable): vague about the problem, unclear target audience, or missing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper: State of the field (required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section describing how the software compares to other commonly-used packages and, when related tools exist, provide a clear 'build vs. contribute' justification explaining the unique scholarly contribution and why existing alternatives are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: thorough comparison and clear explanation of why a new tool was necessary. OK: identifies related work and explains key differences. Bad (not acceptable): ignores existing similar tools or fails to justify why contributing to existing projects wasn't appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper: Software design (required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section explaining architectural choices, trade-offs considered during design, the chosen architecture and why, and why these choices matter for the research application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: thoughtful discussion of design decisions and their implications. OK: clear explanation of architecture with some rationale. Bad (not acceptable): generic code structure description without explaining design reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper: Research impact statement (required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must provide evidence of either realized impact (publications using the software, evidence of external use/adoption, integration with other research tools) OR credible near-term significance (benchmark results demonstrating improvements, reproducible research materials showing capabilities, community-readiness signals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be compelling and specific, not aspirational. Good: multiple citations, documented external users, or strong benchmark results with reproducible materials. OK: some evidence beyond authors' group or solid benchmarks. Bad (not acceptable): only statements about potential future use without concrete evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper: AI usage disclosure (required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section that transparently discloses any use of generative AI in software creation or development, documentation writing, or paper authoring. If no AI tools were used, this should be explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AI tools were used, authors should describe how they were used and how the quality and correctness of AI-generated content was verified. Good: clear, specific disclosure and verification methods. OK: statement that no AI tools were used or general disclosure. Bad (not acceptable): missing section or vague/evasive language about AI usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship plausibility check
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the submitting author has made a 'substantial contribution' to the submitted software (as judged by commit history) and whether the full list of paper authors seems appropriate and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors themselves decide who qualifies for co-authorship; JOSS policy excludes purely financial contributions as sufficient. If the author list seems unexpectedly short or otherwise questionable, raise it as a question during the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations and prior art (novelty and acknowledgement of prior work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that implement solutions already solved in other software packages are acceptable provided they meet JOSS criteria and cite prior similar work; reviewers should point out relevant published work not yet cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If software duplicates existing solutions, authors must cite prior work and justify their contribution (e.g., better design, different target audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer grading guidance (decision categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to grade submissions in one of three categories: 1) Accept 2) Minor Revisions 3) Major Revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS does not reject outright submissions requiring major revisions; reviewers should use these categories to communicate required changes and allow authors time to make modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietary/closed-source environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that rely upon a proprietary/closed source language or development environment are acceptable provided they meet other submission requirements and the reviewer can install the software and verify functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an open source or free variant exists, reviewers are encouraged to suggest authors consider compatibility with that variant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository hosting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Repositories must be hosted at a location that allows outside users to freely open issues and propose code changes (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions will not be accepted if the repository is hosted where accounts must be manually approved or paid for, regardless of who controls approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with JOSS AI/code-generation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS has a detailed policy describing appropriate use of AI by authors and reviewers; reviewers should consult and follow these guidelines before starting the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See referenced JOSS AI policy for scope and expectations (the review page instructs reviewers to review these guidelines before starting).
